q: What is the major product when 2-methylcyclohexanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Acid-catalyzed dehydration goes through a carbocation (E1) and gives the most stable alkene.
w: Protonation of OH and loss of water give a 2° carbocation at C1; a 1,2-hydride shift from C2 gives the 3° cation, and loss of a proton from either cation can form the trisubstituted C=C. E1 dehydration gives the most stable alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexene (disubstituted) forms, but as a minor product; E1 favors the more substituted alkene.
Methylenecyclohexane is a less stable exocyclic, disubstituted alkene and is minor.
4-Methylcyclohexene has the C=C away from the original carbocation site; it would need extra hydride shifts to unproductive 2° cations.

q: 3,3-Dimethyl-2-butanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: The first carbocation is secondary and sits next to a quaternary carbon. What can migrate?
w: Loss of water gives a 2° carbocation at C2. A 1,2-methyl shift from the neighboring quaternary carbon makes a more stable 3° cation, (CH3)2C+–CH(CH3)2. Loss of the lone C–H proton gives the tetrasubstituted alkene 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene, the most stable possible product, as the major product.
x: 3,3-Dimethyl-1-butene is the unrearranged alkene; it is minor because the 2° cation rearranges by a methyl shift before losing a proton.
2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene does come from the rearranged cation, but it is only disubstituted; the tetrasubstituted isomer is major.
With concentrated acid and heat the rearranged cation loses a proton to give the alkene (which leaves the mixture); capture by water is reversed under these conditions.

q: The same alcohol, 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol, is instead treated with POCl<sub>3</sub> in pyridine. What is the major product?
h: Does this reagent pair form a carbocation? Which β carbon still has hydrogens?
w: POCl3 converts OH into a dichlorophosphate leaving group, and pyridine removes a β H in a concerted E2 step. No carbocation forms, so no methyl shift is possible. The only β carbon with hydrogens is C1 (C3 is quaternary), so the product is 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene.
x: 2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene needs a methyl shift, which happens only via a carbocation (acid-catalyzed E1), not in this E2 reaction.
2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene also requires the rearranged skeleton, which a concerted E2 cannot give.
Pyridine is a base, and the phosphate ester is eliminated, not substituted; the alkyl chloride is not the main product.

q: 1-Cyclobutylethanol is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: A carbocation next to a strained four-membered ring can relieve strain by an alkyl (ring bond) shift.
w: Loss of water gives a 2° cation next to the cyclobutane. A ring C–C bond migrates to the cation carbon, expanding the ring to a less strained cyclopentyl cation; that carbon now carries the CH3. A hydride shift (or direct loss of the H on the methyl-bearing carbon) then gives the trisubstituted ring alkene 1-methylcyclopentene.
x: Vinylcyclobutane is the unrearranged, monosubstituted alkene; ring expansion relieves strain and the product is more stable.
Ethylidenecyclobutane keeps the strained four-membered ring and an exocyclic C=C; the ring-expansion pathway wins.
Cyclohexene would need the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon to join the ring as well; ring expansion adds only one carbon (the cation carbon), giving a five-membered ring.

q: Rank the alcohols by rate of acid-catalyzed dehydration (slowest → fastest).
h: The rate-determining step forms a carbocation. Which alcohol gives the most stable one?
w: E1 dehydration is limited by loss of water to form the carbocation, so the rate follows carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1°. I is 3°, II is 2°, III is 1° (which reacts slowly, by an E2-like path). Order: III < II < I.
x: This is reversed; tertiary alcohols dehydrate fastest because they form the most stable carbocations.
The primary alcohol III is the slowest, not the secondary alcohol II.
The tertiary alcohol I is the fastest; 2° alcohol II is slower than I.

q: The energy diagram is for the acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-methyl-2-propanol. Which labeled point is the transition state of the rate-determining step?
h: Match each step: protonation of OH, loss of water, loss of a proton. Which barrier is highest?
w: Step 1 (A) is fast protonation of the OH. Step 2 is loss of water to form the 3° carbocation; its transition state, point B, is the highest point, so this is the rate-determining step. C is the carbocation intermediate (a minimum), and D is the transition state for removal of the β proton.
x: C is an energy minimum, the carbocation intermediate, not a transition state.
A is the transition state for proton transfer to the OH, a fast step with a small barrier.
D is the transition state for loss of the β proton from the carbocation, which is fast compared with ionization.

q: Why is an alcohol dehydrated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> rather than concentrated HBr?
c: Bromide is a good nucleophile and traps the carbocation as an alkyl bromide
HBr is too weak an acid to protonate the alcohol’s OH group
Bromide is a strong base that removes the β proton too slowly to form much alkene
HBr adds water back to the alkene faster than H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> does
h: Compare the conjugate bases: what else can they do to a carbocation?
w: Both acids form the same carbocation. HSO4− and H2PO4− are very poor nucleophiles, so the cation loses a proton (E1). Br− is a good nucleophile and traps the carbocation, so HBr converts alcohols into alkyl bromides (SN1/SN2), not alkenes.
x: HBr (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −9) is a very strong acid and protonates alcohols readily.
Br<sup>−</sup> is a very weak base; the problem is its nucleophilicity, not its basicity.
HBr does not hydrate alkenes; it adds H–Br across the C=C to give an alkyl bromide.

q: Alkene hydration and alcohol dehydration are the reverse of each other. Which set of conditions best favors dehydration to the alkene?
c: Concentrated acid, high temperature, distilling off the alkene
Dilute aqueous acid, low temperature, excess water added to the flask
Concentrated acid, low temperature, excess water added at the start
Dilute aqueous acid, high temperature, a sealed flask so nothing escapes
h: Use Le Châtelier: which side has more molecules, and how can you remove a product?
w: Dehydration makes two molecules from one (ΔS > 0), so high temperature makes −TΔS more favorable. Concentrated acid supplies little water, and distilling the lower-boiling alkene removes a product. So concentrated acid, heat, and removal of the alkene drive the equilibrium to the right.
x: Dilute acid, low temperature and excess water are hydration conditions; they push the equilibrium toward the alcohol.
Excess water and low temperature both favor the alcohol, even with concentrated acid.
In a sealed flask with lots of water, the products cannot leave and water pushes the equilibrium back toward the alcohol.

q: 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide) is heated with AgNO<sub>3</sub> in ethanol. What is the major alkene formed?
c: No alkene forms; this bromide has no β hydrogen
h: Ag<sup>+</sup> pulls off bromide. What does the developing primary cation do next to a quaternary carbon?
w: Ag+ forces ionization; as Br− leaves, a methyl group shifts from the quaternary carbon, giving the 3° 2-methyl-2-butyl cation (no free 1° cation forms). That cation loses a proton (E1) or is trapped by ethanol (SN1). The major alkene is the trisubstituted Zaitsev product, 2-methyl-2-butene.
x: 2-Methyl-1-butene also comes from the rearranged cation, but it is disubstituted and minor.
3-Methyl-1-butene has its C=C two carbons away from the 3° cation center; forming it would require further shifts to less stable 2° and 1° cations.
It is true that the starting bromide has no β H (so no direct E2), but after the methyl shift the 3° cation has β hydrogens and loses one.

q: 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane undergoes E1 when heated in ethanol. Which change would make this reaction faster?
c: Using hexane as the solvent instead of ethanol
h: The rate-determining step of E1 is ionization. What makes ionization easier?
w: E1 rate = k[RX]; the slow step is C–X ionization to the carbocation. A better leaving group speeds this up, so 2-bromo-2-methylbutane reacts faster (Br− is a weaker base and a better leaving group than Cl−).
x: 1-Chloro-3-methylbutane is primary; a 1° carbocation is far too unstable, so it does not undergo E1.
Hexane is nonpolar and cannot stabilize the ions formed in the ionization step, so E1 would be much slower.
2-Chloro-3-methylbutane is secondary; its 2° carbocation forms more slowly than the 3° cation.

q:
Which statements about E1 and E2 reactions are true?
I. E2 normally requires the β H and the leaving group to be anti-periplanar.
II. The rate of an E1 reaction increases when the base concentration is doubled.
III. With small bases, both E1 and E2 usually give mainly the more substituted alkene.
h: Write the rate law for each mechanism, and recall what the transition state of each needs.
w: I is true: the anti-periplanar arrangement lets the C–H σ bond overlap with the C–X σ* orbital in the concerted step. II is false: E1 is first order, rate = k[RX]; the base acts only after the slow step. III is true: E1 goes through a carbocation that loses a proton to give the more stable alkene, and E2 with a small base gives the Zaitsev product. Answer: I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: both pathways favor the Zaitsev alkene when the base is small.
Statement II is false; base is not in the E1 rate-determining step, so rate = k[RX].
Statement II is false; doubling the base does not change an E1 rate.

q: Rank these C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> alkenes from least stable to most stable.
h: More alkyl groups on the C=C stabilize it; for disubstituted alkenes, compare cis and trans.
w: Alkene stability increases with substitution (hyperconjugation, stronger sp2–sp3 bonds), and trans beats cis because cis has steric strain between the groups. III is cis-disubstituted, I is trans-disubstituted, II is tetrasubstituted: III < I < II.
x: The cis isomer (III) is less stable than the trans isomer (I) because its alkyl groups crowd each other.
This is reversed; the tetrasubstituted alkene II is the most stable.
The tetrasubstituted alkene II is more stable than either disubstituted alkene.

q: 1-Butene, (Z)-2-butene and (E)-2-butene all hydrogenate to butane. Their heats of hydrogenation are −127, −120 and −116 kJ/mol (not in order). Which assignment is correct?
h: All three give the same alkane, so the less stable alkene releases more heat.
w: Because all three give the same product, differences in heat released reflect differences in alkene stability: the least stable alkene releases the most heat. Stability: monosubstituted < cis-disubstituted < trans-disubstituted. So 1-butene −127, (Z)-2-butene −120, (E)-2-butene −116 kJ/mol; the E isomer is about 4 kJ/mol more stable than Z.
x: This gives the most heat to the most stable alkene; a more stable alkene sits lower in energy and releases less heat.
The cis isomer is less stable than the trans isomer, so it releases more heat, not less.
1-Butene, the least substituted alkene, is the least stable and releases the most heat.

q: All four alkenes hydrogenate (H2, Pd) to methylcyclohexane. Which one releases the least heat?
h: Same product for all four, so the least heat comes from the most stable alkene.
w: With a common product, the most stable alkene has the smallest heat of hydrogenation. 1-Methylcyclohexene is trisubstituted; the others are disubstituted (3- and 4-methylcyclohexene) or a disubstituted exocyclic alkene (methylenecyclohexane), so 1-methylcyclohexene releases the least heat.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexene is only disubstituted, so it is less stable and releases more heat than the trisubstituted isomer.
4-Methylcyclohexene is disubstituted and releases more heat than 1-methylcyclohexene.
Methylenecyclohexane is a disubstituted exocyclic alkene; it is less stable than 1-methylcyclohexene and releases more heat.

q: Which alkyl bromide gives no E2 product when heated with (CH3)3COK?
h: Every choice has β hydrogens. Where would the new C=C have to be, and can its p orbitals line up?
w: 1-Bromobicyclo[2.2.1]heptane has β hydrogens, but any C=C would have to include the bridgehead carbon. In a small bicyclic ring the bridgehead p orbital cannot overlap with its neighbor's (Bredt's rule), so no E2 occurs. The other three give cyclohexene, methylenecyclohexane (bulky base), and methylenecyclohexane respectively.
x: Bromocyclohexane has axial β H atoms anti to an axial Br in the ring-flipped chair, so it gives cyclohexene.
This 3° bromide eliminates readily; with tert-butoxide it gives mainly methylenecyclohexane.
This 1° bromide has one β H on the ring carbon; the bulky base favors E2 over S<sub>N</sub>2, giving methylenecyclohexane.

q: The heats of hydrogenation of 2,3-dimethyl-1-butene and 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene are about −117 and −111 kJ/mol. Both give 2,3-dimethylbutane. What is ΔH for the isomerization below?
h: Build a Hess's-law cycle through the common alkane.
w: 1-ene → alkane: ΔH = −117; alkane → 2-ene is the reverse of the 2-ene's hydrogenation: ΔH = +111. Sum: −117 + 111 = −6 kJ/mol. The isomerization is exothermic because the tetrasubstituted alkene is more stable.
x: The sign is wrong: going to the more stable (tetrasubstituted) alkene releases energy.
Adding the two heats of hydrogenation double-counts; one of them must be reversed in the cycle.
This both adds the values and flips the sign; reverse only the second hydrogenation, then add.

q: 2-Butanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Which product is formed in the largest amount?
h: Through the carbocation, which C=C is most substituted, and which geometry has less strain?
w: Loss of water gives the 2-butyl cation. Removing a C3 proton gives 2-butene (disubstituted), favored over 1-butene; of the two 2-butenes, the trans isomer has no cis steric strain. E1 picks the most stable alkene, so (E)-2-butene is major.
x: (Z)-2-Butene forms too, but the cis methyl groups make it less stable than the E isomer, so it is minor.
1-Butene is monosubstituted and least stable; it is a minor product of E1.
The ether forms when an alcohol attacks the cation at lower temperature; with heat, elimination dominates.
